title: Tech Millionaires Are Reshaping the Luxury Market With Meteorites, Dinosaurs and Fire Trucks
excerpt: An estimated 440,000 new U.S. millionaires minted by AI and SpaceX windfalls are splashing out on unconventional collectibles, upending traditional luxury brands' playbooks.
body:
• An estimated 440,000 new U.S. millionaires created by stock market gains and AI company IPOs are spending on meteorites, dinosaur fossils, sports teams and fire trucks rather than traditional luxury goods.
  • Three nearly complete dinosaur fossils have sold for over $30 million apiece since 2020, with billionaire Ken Griffin's $44.6 million Stegosaurus purchase setting the all-time record.
  • The personal luxury goods market contracted to €358 billion in 2025, but North America emerged as the fastest-growing region for brands like LVMH, Richemont and Hermès.
  • New tech wealth holders spend about one-third less on apparel and leather goods compared to those with generational wealth, preferring durable assets like real estate, yachts and cars.

Chip, a former SpaceX data scientist sitting on roughly $3.5 million in company stock following the June IPO, recently bought $10,000 worth of meteorites and a $5,000 fire truck. The truck might serve as an attraction at his three-year-old's birthday party. He is not sure yet.

"I've been in T-shirts and shorts for years," the 50-year-old told Reuters. "That's what I'm comfortable in — I don't see that changing."

His spending pattern captures a broader shift that is reshaping the global luxury market. An estimated 440,000 new U.S. millionaires minted by stock market gains and AI company public listings are buying meteorites, dinosaur bones, professional sports teams and smartwatches — and largely bypassing the $406 billion personal luxury goods industry that brands like LVMH, Chanel and Hermès have built over decades.

The Dinosaur Boom

Nowhere is the shift more visible than in the market for prehistoric fossils. Since 2020, three nearly complete dinosaur skeletons have sold for upwards of $30 million apiece at auction. Hedge fund billionaire Kenneth Griffin paid a record $44.6 million for "Apex," a Stegosaurus skeleton, at Sotheby's in 2024. A juvenile Ceratosaurus fetched $30.5 million at Sotheby's New York last July, blowing past its $6 million high estimate after a six-minute bidding war.

In March 2026, a Triceratops fossil dubbed "Trey" sold for $5.55 million on Joopiter, an online auction platform founded by Pharrell Williams, setting a record for a dinosaur skeleton sold in an online-only auction. Crypto investors have also entered the market — Wintermute co-founder Yoann Turpin and a group of crypto investors purchased an intact dinosaur fossil now stored at Singapore's Le Freeport, a facility often described as "Asia's Fort Knox."

"Of all the alternative assets I grew up seeing — wine, art, cars — I think dinosaurs are the most untapped, investment-wise. It's a no-brainer."

— Yoann Turpin, Wintermute co-founder

Different Priorities

The newly wealthy spend about one-third less on apparel and leather goods compared to those with generational wealth, according to Filippo Bianchi, who leads the global luxury team at Boston Consulting Group. Their top spending priority is durable assets: real estate, yachts and cars.

AI strategist Zack Kass, who led OpenAI's go-to-market unit until 2023, used his winnings to buy a professional volleyball team. Former SpaceX engineer Robert and his wife bought Apple Watches and planned an Alaska cruise. A Logan Paul Pikachu Illustrator card sold for $16.5 million in February, smashing the Pokémon card record.

The eclectic spending stands in contrast to the sputtering traditional art market, which posted just 4 percent growth globally last year after declining the year prior, according to the Art Basel and UBS annual report.

Luxury Brands See Opportunity

Despite the unconventional tastes, luxury houses remain cautiously optimistic. North America was among the fastest-growing regions for LVMH, Richemont, Hermès and Kering's Gucci in the quarter ending March 31. Richemont CEO Nicolas Bos attributed the strength to a "high level of consumer confidence in America."

The U.S. was the top destination market for Swiss watches in 2025, accounting for 17 percent of global exports despite tariff disruptions. And high-end mechanical watches retain investment appeal — resale prices often exceed retail.

"You're not wearing your smartwatch with your tux or your suit," said Harrison Colcord, founder of Harrison Lifestyle Concierge, who advises tech clients on luxury purchases.

The Indian Wealth Angle

Indian-origin tech professionals are among the largest beneficiaries of AI-era wealth creation, from senior engineers at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic to founders of generative AI startups. Many are becoming first-generation collectors navigating this rapidly evolving market, where a vintage Pokémon card can outperform a Rembrandt and a dinosaur skeleton costs more than a Picasso.

The personal luxury goods market, valued at €358 billion in 2025, has contracted for two consecutive years, according to Bain & Company. Whether the tech wealth wave can reverse that trend depends on whether brands can adapt to buyers who prefer meteorites to monograms.
nri_angle: Indian-origin tech professionals are among the largest beneficiaries of Silicon Valley and AI-era wealth creation, and many are becoming first-generation collectors navigating this rapidly evolving luxury landscape.
